claim: Evolution is at the core of the impending antibiotic crisis.
source: Evolution is at the core of the impending antibiotic crisis.
evidence: This is a statement drawing from established scientific consensus about antibiotic resistance evolution.

claim: Collateral sensitivity is a phenomenon where evolved resistance to one antibiotic causes hypersensitivity to another one.
source: One option is to exploit evolutionary trade-offs, like collateral sensitivity, where evolved resistance to one antibiotic causes hypersensitivity to another one.
evidence: This is a definition supported by citation to the original work describing the phenomenon.

claim: Bacteria commonly failed to counter hypersensitivity and went extinct in evolution experiments with Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
source: We performed a critical experimental test on this key requirement, using evolution experiments with Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and identified three main outcomes: (i) bacteria commonly failed to counter hypersensitivity and went extinct
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the evolution experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Hypersensitivity sometimes converted into multidrug resistance in evolution experiments with Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
source: (ii) hypersensitivity sometimes converted into multidrug resistance
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the evolution experiments.

claim: Resistance gains frequently caused re-sensitization to the previous drug, thereby maintaining the trade-off.
source: (iii) resistance gains frequently caused re-sensitization to the previous drug, thereby maintaining the trade-off.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the evolution experiments.

claim: Drug order affected the evolutionary outcome in collateral sensitivity experiments.
source: Drug order affected the evolutionary outcome, most likely due to variation in the effect size of collateral sensitivity, epistasis among adaptive mutations, and fitness costs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and inference about the mechanisms.

claim: Treatment of infectious diseases often fails because of the rapid evolution of drug resistance.
source: Treatment of infectious diseases and cancer often fail because of the rapid evolution of drug resistance (Bloemberg et al., 2015; Davies and Davies, 2010; Gottesman, 2002; Zaretsky et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Evolved collateral sensitivity is pervasive in laboratory strains and clinical isolates of distinct bacterial species.
source: Recent large-scale studies have demonstrated that evolved collateral sensitivity is pervasive in laboratory strains and clinical isolates of distinct bacterial species (Barbosa et al., 2017; Imamovic et al., 2018; Imamovic and Sommer, 2013; Jansen et al., 2016; Jiao et al., 2016; Lázár et al., 2014; Lázár et al., 2013; Oz et al., 2014; Podnecky et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Evolved collateral sensitivity is pervasive in cancer cells.
source: as well as cancer cells (Dhawan et al., 2017; Pluchino et al., 2012; Shaw et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on cancer cells.

claim: Evolved collateral sensitivity can slow down resistance evolution during combination therapy.
source: More importantly, evolved collateral sensitivity can slow down resistance evolution during combination (Barbosa et al., 2018; Rodriguez de Evgrafov et al., 2015; Munck et al., 2014) and sequential therapy (Kim et al., 2014; Roemhild et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Evolved collateral sensitivity can slow down resistance evolution during sequential therapy.
source: More importantly, evolved collateral sensitivity can slow down resistance evolution during combination (Barbosa et al., 2018; Rodriguez de Evgrafov et al., 2015; Munck et al., 2014) and sequential therapy (Kim et al., 2014; Roemhild et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Evolved collateral sensitivity can limit the spread of plasmid-borne resistance genes.
source: and also limit the spread of plasmid-borne resistance genes (Rosenkilde et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Recent work identified evolution of contrasting collateral effects for different bacteria, including Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
source: Recent work even identified evolution of contrasting collateral effects (i.e., some populations with evolved collateral sensitivity and others with cross-resistance) for different bacteria, including Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Barbosa et al., 2017), Escherichia coli (Nichol et al., 2019; Oz et al., 2014), Enterococcus faecalis (Maltas and Wood, 2019), and a BCR-ABL leukemeia cell line (Zhao et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Contrasting collateral effects are likely due to the stochastic nature of mutations combined with alternative evolutionary paths to resistance.
source: These patterns are likely due to the stochastic nature of mutations combined with alternative evolutionary paths to resistance against the first selective drug, subsequently causing distinct collateral effects against other drugs (Barbosa et al., 2017; Nichol et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is an inference supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: An antibiotic pair that consistently produced collateral sensitivity in small Staphylococcus aureus populations produced complete cross-resistance in large populations.
source: For example, an antibiotic pair, which consistently produced collateral sensitivity in small Staphylococcus aureus populations (e.g., 106), instead produced complete cross-resistance in large populations (e.g., 109) and thus an escape from the evolutionary constraint, most likely due to the higher likelihood of advantageous rare mutations under these conditions (Jiao et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Ciprofloxacin-resistance lineages of P. aeruginosa showed increased sensitivity to piperacillin and tobramycin.
source: As part of the results, the authors identified lineages with evolved resistance against ciprofloxacin that simultaneously showed increased sensitivity to piperacillin and tobramycin.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to a previous study (Yen and Papin, 2017).

claim: Exposure of ciprofloxacin-resistance lineages to either piperacillin or tobramycin led to the evolution of resistance against these two antibiotics and substantial re-sensitization to ciprofloxacin.
source: The subsequent exposure of the ciprofloxacin-resistance lineages to either piperacillin or tobramycin led to the evolution of resistance against these two antibiotics and substantial (yet not complete) re-sensitization to ciprofloxacin.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to a previous study (Yen and Papin, 2017).

claim: The evolution of multidrug resistance was only prevented in treatments with polymyxin B that were characterized by evolved collateral sensitivity in E. coli populations evolved in a morbidostat.
source: The evolution of multidrug resistance was only prevented in the two treatments with polymyxin B that were also characterized by evolved collateral sensitivity, although again only in one direction (Yoshida et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The study used previously evolved, highly resistant P. aeruginosa populations obtained from serial passage experiments with increasing concentrations of clinically relevant bactericidal antibiotics.
source: We took advantage of previously evolved, highly resistant P. aeruginosa populations, which we obtained from serial passage experiments with increasing concentrations of clinically relevant bactericidal antibiotics (drug A, Figure 1a) (Barbosa et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental material used, supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Two cases of reciprocal collateral sensitivity were identified: piperacillin/tazobactam and streptomycin, and carbenicillin and gentamicin.
source: From these, we identified two cases of reciprocal collateral sensitivity, including (i) piperacillin/tazobactam (PIT) and streptomycin (STR), or (ii) carbenicillin (CAR) and gentamicin (GEN).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The reciprocity of collateral effects was re-assessed using dose-response analysis.
source: In the current study, we now re-assessed the reciprocity of collateral effects using dose-response analysis (Figure 1b and c, Supplementary file 1–Figure 1–supplementary table 1, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim describes a method used in the study and references figures showing the data.

claim: The imposed antibiotic selection frequently caused population extinction.
source: The imposed antibiotic selection frequently caused population extinction (Figure 2, Figure 2—source data 1), even though sublethal drug concentrations were used.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Extinction events occurred significantly more often when selection for the original resistance was maintained by the presence of both drugs.
source: Extinction events occurred significantly more often when selection for the original resistance was maintained by the presence of both drugs (extinction in constrained treatments vs. only one drug, χ2 = 12.9, df = 1, p<0.0001; Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In treatments with only the second drug B, extinction occurred significantly more often under strong, but not mild concentration increases.
source: In treatments with only the second drug B, extinction occurred significantly more often under strong, but not mild concentration increases (strong vs. mild increases in unconstrained environments, χ2 = 5.5, df = 1, p=0.019).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Drug switches with the antibiotic pair STR/PIT produced 33 extinction events (~51%).
source: Drug switches with the antibiotic pair STR/PIT was particularly successful, with 33 extinction events (~51%, Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The CAR/GEN pair produced only seven extinctions (~10%), all restricted to one drug order, GEN>CAR.
source: The results differed for the CAR/GEN pair, which produced only seven extinctions (~10%), all restricted to one drug order, GEN>CAR, suggesting asymmetry in the ability to counter collateral sensitivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and includes an inference about asymmetry.

claim: Both combinations PIT/STR and CAR/GEN are synergistic against P. aeruginosa.
source: The observed differences in the extinction levels of the pairs considered here are unlikely to be the result of differences in combined synergy, since both combinations (PIT/STR and CAR/GEN) are synergistic against P. aeruginosa (Barbosa et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Bacterial adaptation increased in all surviving populations of the CAR/GEN pair.
source: We measured bacterial adaptation using relative biomass (see Materials and methods and Roemhild et al., 2018) and found it to have increased in all surviving populations (Figure 3a and b, Supplementary file 1–Figure 3–supplementary table 1, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: For both drug orders, the increase in relative biomass was significantly slower in the constrained treatments.
source: For both drug orders, the increase was significantly slower in the constrained treatments, and, to a lesser extent, for the strong concentration increases (Figure 3a and b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The CAR>GEN switch maintained a high relative biomass across time.
source: Consistent with the asymmetry in extinction, the CAR>GEN switch (with no extinction) maintained a high relative biomass across time, while the reverse direction GEN>CAR (with extinction) produced lower relative biomass levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and inference about the relationship to extinction.

claim: All surviving populations of the CAR/GEN pair significantly increased resistance against the second drug.
source: In detail, all surviving populations significantly increased resistance against the second drug (IC90-fold change between two and >64 times that of the starting populations; Figure 3c and d, Supplementary file 1–Figure 3–supplementary tables 2 and 3, Figure 3—source data 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: In the CAR>GEN switch, all populations maintained their original resistance, yielding bacteria with multidrug resistance.
source: In the suboptimal switch, CAR>GEN, all populations maintained their original resistance, thereby yielding bacteria with multidrug resistance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: In the GEN>CAR switch, the original resistance was only maintained when both drugs were present in combination (constrained environments).
source: This was different for the alternative direction GEN>CAR, where the original resistance was only maintained when both drugs were present in combination (constrained environments).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Under unconstrained evolution in the GEN>CAR switch, cases of significant re-sensitization to the first drug were observed.
source: Only under unconstrained evolution, we observed cases of significant re-sensitization to the first drug.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The starting clones for the second evolution experiment showed significantly impaired growth rates under drug-free conditions, with up to 50% reductions relative to the ancestor.
source: The starting clones for the second evolution experiment indeed showed significantly impaired growth rates under drug-free conditions, with up to 50% reductions relative to the ancestor (Barbosa et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from a previous study.

claim: For the GEN>CAR switch, there was a significant increase in growth rate relative to the wild type PA14 in the unconstrained treatments.
source: For the GEN>CAR switch, we indeed found a significant increase in growth rate relative to the wild type PA14 in the unconstrained treatments (Figure 3f, Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Constrained populations for the GEN>CAR switch showed a significantly reduced growth rate relative to PA14, but with significantly improved values relative to the starting population.
source: Constrained populations for this particular switch still showed a significantly reduced growth rate relative to PA14, with however significantly improved values relative to the starting population (Figure 3f, Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The evolution of multidrug resistance in the CAR>GEN switch can be explained by the sequential fixation of mutations including those in ptsP under unconstrained conditions.
source: Our results reveal that the evolution of multidrug resistance in the suboptimal switch CAR>GEN can be explained by the sequential fixation of mutations including, under unconstrained conditions, those in ptsP (Figure 4a, Figure 4—source data 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic data shown in Figure 4.

claim: ptsP is a main component of the global regulatory system of ABC transporters and other virulence factors.
source: ptsP (Figure 4a, Figure 4—source data 1), a main component of the global regulatory system of ABC transporters and other virulence factors (Feinbaum et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Under constrained conditions in the CAR>GEN switch, mutations were found in the NADH-dehydrogenase genes nuoD or nuoG.
source: Similarly, under constrained conditions, we found mutations in the NADH-dehydrogenase genes nuoD or nuoG (Figure 4a, Figure 4—source data 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Inactivation of nuoD or nuoG is known to influence proton motive force and resistance against aminoglycosides.
source: which are known to influence proton motive force and resistance against aminoglycosides upon inactivation (El'Garch et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Multidrug resistance in the constrained GEN>CAR treatments coincided with mutations in mexR, phoQ, and cpxS.
source: For the more effective switch GEN>CAR, multidrug resistance in the constrained treatments coincided with mutations in mexR, phoQ, and cpxS, an independent regulator of MexAB-OprM (Li et al., 2016) and two-component regulators involved in aminoglycoside resistance (Gooderham and Hancock, 2009) and envelope stress response (Roemhild et al., 2018), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic data and citations to previous literature.

claim: Re-sensitization towards the first drug in the unconstrained GEN>CAR treatments was associated with mutations in nalC and nalD that upregulate the expression of the multidrug-efflux system MexAB-OprM.
source: The re-sensitization towards the first drug in the unconstrained GEN>CAR treatments was associated with two main types of mutational changes at high frequencies across several replicates, including (i) mutations in nalC and nalD that upregulate the expression of the multidrug-efflux system MexAB-OprM in P. aeruginosa (Li et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic data and a citation to previous literature.

claim: Re-sensitization towards the first drug in the unconstrained GEN>CAR treatments was associated with large deletions in pmrB.
source: and (ii) large deletions in pmrB, which is part of a two-component regulatory system (Figure 4b, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Mutations in nalC were previously shown to mediate both resistance to CAR and hypersensitivity to GEN.
source: Mutations in nalC were previously shown to mediate both resistance to CAR and hypersensitivity to GEN (Barbosa et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Re-sensitization to GEN may be caused by antagonistic pleiotropy of nalC mutations that override the resistance of the original pmrB mutation.
source: Thus, re-sensitization to GEN may be caused by antagonistic pleiotropy of nalC mutations that override the resistance of the original pmrB mutation (Figure 4, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the genomic data.

claim: The pmrB mutant had half of the MIC of PA14 on CAR, confirming collateral sensitivity.
source: On CAR, the pmrB mutant had half of the MIC of PA14 (confirming collateral sensitivity), whilst nalC and nalD mutants had increased resistance to CAR.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from functional genetic analysis.

claim: nalC and nalD mutants had increased resistance to CAR.
source: whilst nalC and nalD mutants had increased resistance to CAR.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from functional genetic analysis.

claim: The double mutants had lower MIC on CAR than the nalC and nalD single mutants.
source: The double mutants had lower MIC on CAR than the nalC and nalD single mutants (Figure 4c, Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The extent of MIC changes in the double mutants corresponded to the product of the individual effects in the respective single mutants on CAR, indicating an additive interaction among mutations.
source: The extent of MIC changes in the double mutants corresponded to the product of the individual effects in the respective single mutants, thus indicating an additive interaction among mutations on CAR.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and inference about the type of interaction.

claim: On GEN, the double mutants had substantially lower MICs than expected from the single mutants, strongly suggesting negative epistasis.
source: On GEN, however, the double mutants had substantially lower MICs than expected from the single mutants (Figure 4d, Figure 4—source data 2), strongly suggesting negative epistasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and inference about epistasis.

claim: The pmrB, nalD double mutant had 3x lower MIC to GEN than expected from the individual effects.
source: The pmrB, nalD double mutant had 3x lower MIC to GEN than expected from the individual effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from functional genetic analysis.

claim: The pmrB, nalC double mutant had >30 x lower MIC to GEN than expected from the individual effects, resulting in greater sensitivity than PA14.
source: The pmrB, nalC double mutant had >30 x lower MIC to GEN than expected from the individual effects, resulting in greater sensitivity than PA14 (Figure 4d, Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Re-sensitization to GEN is mediated by antagonistic pleiotropy and negative epistasis.
source: Altogether, we conclude that re-sensitization to GEN is mediated by antagonistic pleiotropy and negative epistasis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data from functional genetic analysis.

claim: Extinction events were frequent in the validation experiment and occurred significantly more often when selection for the original resistance was maintained by the presence of both drugs.
source: Our validation experiment now demonstrated that extinction events were frequent and occurred significantly more often when selection for the original resistance was maintained by the presence of both drugs (extinction in constrained vs. strong environments, χ2 = 16.204, df = 1, p<0.0001; Figure 5b; Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the validation experiment shown in Figure 5.

claim: CIP-resistant populations all survived when challenged with either of the aminoglycosides (STR, GEN).
source: For example, CIP-resistant populations all survived when challenged with either of the aminoglycosides (STR, GEN), whereas more than 50% of these populations went extinct when exposed to β-lactams (CAR, PIT, Figure 5b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: More than 50% of CIP-resistant populations went extinct when exposed to β-lactams (CAR, PIT).
source: whereas more than 50% of these populations went extinct when exposed to β-lactams (CAR, PIT, Figure 5b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Variation in extinction was significantly associated with only the molecular target of the second antibiotic.
source: Our analysis revealed that variation in extinction was significantly associated with only the molecular target of the second antibiotic (GLM, combined extinction, n = 14 drug switches, F = 11.016, p=0.011; Supplementary file 1–Figure 6–supplementary table 1, Figure 6—source data 1), but not with growth rate, extent of collateral sensitivity, or target of the first antibiotic.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Extinction frequencies were on average twice as high in the six treatments that switched to β-lactam antibiotics that target the cell wall, as compared to the eight treatments that switched to aminoglycoside antibiotics that target the ribosome.
source: Extinction frequencies were on average twice as high in the six treatments that switched to β-lactam antibiotics that target the cell wall, as compared to the eight treatments that switched to aminoglycoside antibiotics that target the ribosome (Figure 6a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Resistance gains to drug B were frequently associated with re-sensitization to the original drug A in the unconstrained treatments.
source: Resistance gains to drug B were frequently associated with re-sensitization to the original drug A in the unconstrained treatments, while resistance to the new drug B increased in all 14 tested cases
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the validation experiment.

claim: Resistance to the new drug B increased in all 14 tested cases in the validation experiment.
source: while resistance to the new drug B increased in all 14 tested cases (leading to changes of 2 up to >64 times the IC90 of the starting populations; Supplementary file 1–Figure 5–supplementary tables 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the validation experiment.

claim: Significant antibiotic re-sensitization was observed for 5 of the 14 cases (36%) in the validation experiment.
source: In detail, we observed significant antibiotic re-sensitization for 5 of the 14 cases (36%, Figure 5b, Figure 5—source data 3, Supplementary file 1–Figure 5–supplementary table 1, Figure 5—source data 1
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Re-sensitization did not occur in the constrained treatments in the validation experiment.
source: Re-sensitization did not occur in the constrained treatments.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the validation experiment.

claim: The extent of re-sensitization in the unconstrained treatments was significantly associated with the target of drug A.
source: Our statistical analysis revealed that the extent of re-sensitization in the unconstrained treatments was significantly associated to equal degrees with the target of drug A (GLM, resistance against drug A, n = 14, F = 15.27, p=0.0019; Supplementary file 1–Figure 6–supplementary table 2, Figure 6—source data 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The extent of re-sensitization in the unconstrained treatments was significantly associated with the effect size of collateral sensitivity.
source: the effect size of collateral sensitivity (F = 15.91, p=0.004)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The extent of re-sensitization in the unconstrained treatments was significantly associated with growth rate in drug-free media.
source: and growth rate in drug-free media (F = 18.38, p=0.0027)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Re-sensitization was stronger in drug switches that started with an aminoglycoside, as compared to β-lactam, and fluoroquinolone.
source: Re-sensitization was stronger in drug switches that started with an aminoglycoside, as compared to β-lactam, and fluoroquinolone (Figure 6b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The extent of resistance gains in unconstrained treatments was significantly associated with the initial effect size of collateral sensitivity.
source: In contrast, the extent of resistance gains in unconstrained treatments was not associated with drug targets of either drug A or B, but instead significantly associated with both the initial effect size of collateral sensitivity (GLM, resistance against drug B, n = 14, F = 6.71, p=0.0321; Supplementary file 1-Figure 6–supplementary table 2, Figure 6—source data 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The extent of resistance gains in unconstrained treatments was significantly associated with the initial growth rate of the resistant population in drug-free media.
source: and the initial growth rate of the resistant population in drug-free media (GLM, resistance against drug B, n = 14, F = 7.90, p=0.0228).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Collateral sensitivity effect size showed a negative association with the resistance gains to drug B.
source: Collateral sensitivity effect size showed a negative association with the resistance gains to drug B (Figure 6c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: High sensitivity appears to be prone to more rapid resistance gains, possibly because it opens a fitness space for rapid adaptation.
source: High sensitivity thus appears to be prone to more rapid resistance gains, possibly because it opens a fitness space for rapid adaptation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: The population resistance changes against drug B were generally larger than the initial collateral sensitivity.
source: The population resistance changes against drug B were generally larger than the initial collateral sensitivity (Figure 5b; Figure 5—source data 3); Supplementary file 1-Figure 5-supplementary tables 1-2; evolved lineages showed higher resistance than the PA14 wild type), indicating that they were not solely due to competition of pre-existing sub-populations, but involved new genetic adaptations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and inference about the mechanism.

claim: The presence of a general adaptation trade-off inhibited rapid adaptation.
source: As observed above, the presence of a general adaptation trade-off (measured as reduction in growth rate relative to ancestral PA14 in drug-free environments) inhibited rapid adaptation (Figure 6d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The stability of collateral sensitivity switching is shaped predominantly by drug targets, but additionally influenced by the effect size of collateral sensitivity and a general adaptation trade-off.
source: Taken together, our results at the population level suggest that the stability of collateral sensitivity switching is shaped predominantly by drug targets, but additionally influenced by the effect size of collateral sensitivity and a general adaptation trade-off.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data from the validation experiment.

claim: The most stable collateral sensitivity was identified for the switch from aminoglycoside to β-lactam.
source: The most stable collateral sensitivity was identified for the switch from aminoglycoside to β-lactam.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Within a particular drug switch, the highest stability was achieved for low collateral sensitivity effect sizes.
source: Within a particular drug switch, the highest stability was achieved for low collateral sensitivity effect sizes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Large adaptation trade-offs tended to inhibit evolutionary change, that is both desirable re-sensitization, and new resistance.
source: Large adaptation trade-offs tended to inhibit evolutionary change, that is both desirable re-sensitization, and new resistance.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Evolved reciprocal collateral sensitivity generally limited bacterial adaptation.
source: Evolved reciprocal collateral sensitivity generally limited bacterial adaptation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Adaptation was particularly constrained in treatments that switched to a β-lactam, as reflected by the elevated extinction rates.
source: Adaptation was particularly constrained in treatments that switched to a β-lactam, as reflected by the elevated extinction rates.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: The effect was strongest when the first antibiotic was maintained and a second was added.
source: The effect was strongest when the first antibiotic was maintained and a second was added.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Extinction rates are often not reported as an evolutionary outcome in related studies.
source: Interestingly, extinction rates are often not reported as an evolutionary outcome in related studies, possibly because of a different main focus of the study (Yen and Papin, 2017), or because extinction could not be recorded due to the particular experimental set-up (i.e., usage of a morbidostat; Yoshida et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an observation about the literature with citations.

claim: Extinction frequencies are known from previous evolution experiments to vary among treatment types.
source: Considering that antimicrobial therapy usually aims at elimination of bacterial pathogens and extinction frequencies are known from previous evolution experiments to vary among treatment types (Barbosa et al., 2018; Hansen et al., 2017; Roemhild et al., 2018; Torella et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: High relative stability for collateral sensitivity treatments switching from an aminoglycoside to a β-lactam was observed in both datasets (clonal and population-level evolution).
source: In both datasets (clonal and population-level evolution), we observed high relative stability for collateral sensitivity treatments switching from an aminoglycoside to a β-lactam.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data from both datasets.

claim: The stability of the aminoglycoside to β-lactam switch may be caused by slower adaptation and efficient re-sensitization.
source: Our detailed analysis for the CAR/GEN pair at the clonal level demonstrates that this stability may be caused by slower adaptation (Figure 3a), and efficient re-sensitization (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The slow adaptation rates may be the result of selection favoring the reversal of two evolutionary trade-offs together with a relative paucity of accessible resistance mutations.
source: Also, the slow adaptation rates may be the result of selection favoring the reversal of two evolutionary trade-offs (Figures 3e and 6d) together with a relative paucity of accessible resistance mutations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: The efficient re-sensitization observed during switches from an aminoglycoside to a β-lactam may be explained by pleiotropy and drug-specific negative epistasis.
source: The efficient re-sensitization that was observed during switches from an aminoglycoside to a β-lactam may be explained by pleiotropy and drug-specific negative epistasis (Figure 4c and d).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Collateral sensitivity treatments that switch to aminoglycosides tended to show lower stability, as reflected by the lower levels of extinction and the lack of re-sensitization.
source: On the other hand, collateral sensitivity treatments that switch to aminoglycosides, tended to show lower stability, as reflected by the lower levels of extinction (Figure 6a) and the lack of re-sensitization (Figure 6b) at the population level.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The collateral sensitivity treatments CAR>STR and CIP>STR were frequently countered by the evolving bacteria.
source: For instance, the collateral sensitivity treatments CAR>STR and CIP>STR were frequently countered by the evolving bacteria.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Small values for a general adaptation trade-off accelerated adaptation.
source: While our data cannot fully explain the high instability, it appears that small values for a general adaptation trade-off (i.e., indicated by reduced growth rates in drug-free environments), which are also frequently observed for CIP resistance mutations (Huseby et al., 2017), accelerated adaptation (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 6 and citation to previous literature.

claim: The expression of particular collateral sensitivity mutations strongly depended on the genetic background and could even cause opposite effects in the closely related species of E. coli and Salmonella enterica due to epistasis.
source: A recent publication confirmed that the expression of particular collateral sensitivity mutations strongly depended on the genetic background and could even cause opposite effects in the closely related species of E. coli and Salmonella enterica due to epistasis (Apjok et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a recent publication.

claim: Epistasis is of high importance for the temporal stability of antibiotic sensitivity.
source: Our work on the GEN>CAR switch now shows, that epistasis is of high importance also for the temporal stability of antibiotic sensitivity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data from the GEN>CAR switch.

claim: Drug re-sensitization in the unconstrained GEN>CAR treatments was likely dependent on negative epistasis among pleiotropic resistance mutations.
source: Here, drug re-sensitization in the unconstrained treatments was likely dependent on negative epistasis among pleiotropic resistance mutations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: Mutations in pmrB and the efflux regulators nalC and nalD interacted negatively with each other and caused a complete re-sensitization of bacteria that were previously resistant against GEN.
